title: An efficient framework for uncertainty propagation in nonlinear reinforced concrete analysis using multiplicative dimension reduction and laplace-transform maximum entropy
content:
by Marzieh Allahyari, Masoud Soltani

Uncertainty in material properties, member geometry, and modeling assumptions can strongly affect the predicted response of reinforced concrete (RC) structures, especially after cracking, yielding, and other nonlinear mechanisms develop. Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) provides a direct reference for uncertainty propagation, but its computational cost can become prohibitive when each realization requires an iterative nonlinear finite-element analysis. Dimension-reduction methods can estimate response moments using fewer deterministic analyses, while maximum-entropy methods can reconstruct probability distributions from limited probabilistic information. However, the accuracy, computational efficiency, and practical applicability of an integrated dimension-reduction and maximum-entropy workflow have not been sufficiently established for nonlinear fiber-based RC member and frame analysis. This paper implements and evaluates a non-intrusive uncertainty-propagation workflow that combines the multiplicative dimension reduction method (M-DRM) with a Laplace-transform fractional-moment maximum entropy method (LT-FM-MEM). The workflow communicates with a nonlinear fiber-based finite-element solver through input and output files, requiring no solver modification. Its performance is evaluated using the Huang–Du I-section beam benchmark, an RC cantilever column, and the Vecchio–Emara frame. MCS is used as the numerical reference method, while first-order second-moment (FOSM) analysis is included as a low-cost local-linear comparison. In the two-variable cantilever cases, M-DRM required 15 deterministic analyses, compared with 600 MCS analyses (approximately 40 times fewer). Distribution comparisons at the selected cantilever response levels give Kolmogorov–Smirnov distances of approximately 0.06–0.08 and 95th-quantile errors of approximately 1.3–3.7% for the M-DRM + LT-FM-MEM reconstructions. For the Huang–Du benchmark at m = 4, the KS distance is approximately 0.0064, and the 95th-quantile error is approximately 0.30%. For the Vecchio–Emara frame, the isolated steel-yield-strength uncertainty scenario produces greater response dispersion than the isolated concrete-strength and section-dimension scenarios under the assigned input distributions. These results support the integrated workflow as a reduced-cost approach for distribution-level uncertainty assessment of the investigated nonlinear RC systems.
